script.opening: "For the last few months my feet have felt numb and tingly, like walking on cotton wool, and it’s slowly creeping up my legs — and now the tips of my fingers are starting too. It’s both sides. I stubbed my toe badly last week and barely felt it. What’s causing it, doc?"

facts.text: Started about 6 months ago in both feet at the same time — "pins and needles in the toes". Slowly crept up to just above the ankles, both sides the same. Fingertips tingly for the last month. Burning in the feet at night sometimes. "Like walking on cotton wool."

No weakness — can climb stairs and grip normally. A bit unsteady "in the dark, when I can’t see my feet". No falls. No trouble breathing or swallowing. Nothing has got worse quickly; it’s been gradual over months.

No back pain, no bladder or bowel problems, no dizziness on standing, no erection problems he’ll admit to unless asked directly ("not as good as it was"). Thirsty and passing water more at night for a few months. No weight loss. No rashes.

If asked gently: "More than I should." About 4–5 pints of strong lager most evenings and more at weekends — "maybe 60 or 70 units a week if I’m honest". Has a drink most mornings "to settle my hands" only if asked about morning drinking. Never had a fit or the shakes badly. Has never tried to stop.
Eats "whatever’s quick" — lots of takeaways, not much fruit or veg. Takes no regular medicines and no vitamins. No allergies. No chemotherapy ever. Never been tested for diabetes.

If asked: the practice nurse checked his feet and blood pressure this morning before the video call — "she poked my feet with a nylon wire and I couldn’t feel most of it, and she said the tuning fork wasn’t felt at my big toes. She said my pulses were fine and there were no sores."
Divorced, lives alone in a flat. Works as a forklift driver in a warehouse (needs to feel the pedals). Smokes 10 a day. Father had diabetes and "lost a toe". No one in the family with nerve problems.
Stubbed his right big toe on a door frame last week; noticed it was bruised and bleeding only when he took his sock off. It has healed.

Practical, a bit gruff, worried underneath. Downplay the drinking unless asked in a non-judgemental way; if lectured, become defensive ("everyone at work drinks"). If the doctor explains clearly and offers help, admit you’ve wondered if the drink is to blame and agree to bloods.

ice.ideas: "Is it my circulation? Or is it the drink? I did wonder about the drink."
ice.concerns: "My dad lost a toe with his diabetes. I’m scared I’ll end up in a wheelchair, or lose my job if I can’t feel the pedals on the forklift."
ice.expectations: "Find out what it is and give me something for it." Will accept blood tests; not expecting to talk about drinking.

cues: "I stubbed my toe and barely felt it" — loss of protective sensation; foot-care advice needed.
"More than I should, if I’m honest" — the door to quantifying alcohol, done without judgement.
"Dad lost a toe with his diabetes" — family history pointing to diabetes, and his fear.

checkpoints.text: Recognises a GLOVE-AND-STOCKING peripheral (length-dependent sensory) NEUROPATHY — symmetrical distal numbness/tingling starting in the feet, ascending, now in the fingertips — with reduced sensation

SYSTEMATICALLY searches for the CAUSE — diabetes (HbA1c), alcohol excess, B12/folate deficiency, hypothyroidism, renal/liver disease, drugs/toxins, and less common inflammatory/paraprotein/hereditary causes — directed by history

Uses the recorded foot findings (monofilament, vibration, pulses, skin) and what video allows (gait, balance), and arranges a face-to-face examination of reflexes/ankle jerks, power/wasting and proprioception and distinguishes from mononeuropathy/radiculopathy/central causes

Orders TARGETED investigations (HbA1c/glucose, B12/folate, U&E, LFTs/GGT, TFTs, FBC, ESR; consider protein electrophoresis/paraprotein and HIV; thiamine given on NICE CG100 criteria rather than tested) and nerve conduction/neurology if cause unclear/atypical

Recognises RED FLAGS (rapidly progressive/ascending weakness — Guillain-Barré; motor-predominant, asymmetric, autonomic, acute) needing urgent referral, and refers neurology where unclear/atypical/severe

Manages MODIFIABLE causes (alcohol reduction after AUDIT, without sudden cessation if dependent, NICE CG115, + thiamine on NICE CG100 criteria, glycaemic control, B12/folate/thyroid replacement) and gives FOOT-CARE/safety advice (injury/burn/ulcer risk) ± neuropathic-pain treatment (NICE CG173)
Takes the symptoms seriously, explores and addresses alcohol/glycaemia honestly but NON-JUDGEMENTALLY, and explains the cause-search plan clearly

Safety-nets and follows up: red flags warranting urgent review (progressive/ascending weakness, breathing/swallowing problems), results and any neurology referral, foot-care safety, modifiable-cause plan, and review — finding the cause, not just labelling neuropathy

worked.txt: "What you’re describing — numbness starting in both feet, creeping up, now in your fingertips, and not feeling that stubbed toe — is a nerve problem we call a peripheral neuropathy, in a ‘glove-and-stocking’ pattern. The important job now is to find WHY, because that guides treatment."

"The common causes are diabetes, heavy alcohol, low vitamin B12, and thyroid problems, among others. Can we talk honestly about your drinking — it’s relevant, not a telling-off? I’ll ask a few standard questions about how much you drink. And I’ll check your blood sugar, B12, thyroid, kidneys and liver."

"The nurse’s check this morning shows the feeling is reduced up to your ankles. Could you stand up and walk across the room for me? I’d also like you in this week so I can check your reflexes and strength in person — that tells me how far it’s gone and helps pin the cause."

"One thing I need to ask: any actual WEAKNESS, or is it spreading quickly upward, any trouble breathing or swallowing? … No. If that ever happened it would be urgent — but your gradual, sensation-only pattern is more typical of the common causes."

"The good news: several causes are treatable — cutting down alcohol — safely, because stopping suddenly can be dangerous if your body is used to it — with a vitamin called thiamine if you need it, controlling sugar, replacing B12. And because you can’t feel injuries well, check your feet daily, mind hot water and good footwear, to avoid burns and ulcers."

"I’ll get the bloods, and if the cause isn’t clear or anything’s unusual, I’ll refer you to neurology for nerve tests. Come back urgently if you develop weakness, it climbs quickly, or you get breathing or swallowing trouble. We’ll review the results together."

f.learning: SYMMETRICAL, distal, length-dependent sensory loss and tingling that starts in the FEET and ascends, later involving the hands ("GLOVE-AND-STOCKING"), with reduced sensation (including unnoticed injury) and diminished ankle reflexes, is the classic pattern of a peripheral (typically sensory) POLYNEUROPATHY — and the core skill is to SEARCH SYSTEMATICALLY FOR THE CAUSE rather than simply apply the label. The major causes are DIABETES (the commonest — check HbA1c), ALCOHOL excess, vitamin B12/folate DEFICIENCY, HYPOTHYROIDISM, chronic kidney/liver disease, and DRUGS/TOXINS, with less common inflammatory/immune (CIDP), paraproteinaemia/myeloma, vasculitic and hereditary causes; the history (alcohol intake, diabetes risk, drugs, diet, family history) directs the work-up. Use recorded findings (monofilament, vibration, foot pulses and skin) and what video shows (gait, balance), and arrange a face-to-face examination of reflexes, any weakness/wasting and proprioception, plus signs of an underlying cause, distinguishing a length-dependent neuropathy from mononeuropathy/radiculopathy and central causes. Order targeted tests — HbA1c/glucose, B12/folate, U&E, LFTs/GGT, TFTs, FBC, ESR, with serum protein electrophoresis/paraprotein and HIV considered (thiamine is given on NICE CG100 criteria rather than measured) — and use nerve conduction studies/neurology referral where the cause is unclear, the pattern atypical, or features severe. Recognise RED FLAGS needing urgent assessment: rapidly progressive or ASCENDING weakness (Guillain-Barré syndrome — a neurological emergency, monitor breathing/bulbar function), prominent motor involvement, marked asymmetry, autonomic features or acute onset. Manage the MODIFIABLE causes (alcohol reduction — AUDIT, and no sudden stop if dependent, NICE CG115 — with thiamine on NICE CG100 criteria, glycaemic control, B12/folate/thyroid replacement), give FOOT-CARE/safety advice given the injury/burn/ulcer risk, treat neuropathic pain if present (NICE CG173), and address alcohol/glycaemia honestly but non-judgementally.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG239 (vitamin B12 deficiency in over 16s, 2024) · [2] NICE NG28 (type 2 diabetes in adults, updated) · [3] NICE NG19 (diabetic foot problems, 2015, updated) · [4] NICE CG115 (alcohol-use disorders: diagnosis, assessment and management of harmful drinking and alcohol dependence, 2011) · [5] NICE CG100 (alcohol-use disorders: physical complications, 2010, updated) · [6] NICE CG173 (neuropathic pain in adults: pharmacological management in non-specialist settings, 2013, updated 2020) · [7] UK Chief Medical Officers’ low-risk drinking guidelines (2016) · [8] DVLA Assessing fitness to drive: a guide for medical professionals (current edition)
knowledge.summary: Symmetrical numbness and tingling that starts in the feet, climbs the legs and then reaches the fingertips is a length-dependent sensory polyneuropathy — the glove-and-stocking pattern. The label is the easy part. The station is about finding the cause (diabetes, alcohol, B12 or folate deficiency, thyroid, kidney or liver disease, drugs, paraprotein), screening for the rare emergency (Guillain–Barré), protecting his numb feet, and talking about alcohol without judgement.

points.t: Distal, symmetrical, feet before hands, slowly progressive over months, sensory more than motor: a length-dependent polyneuropathy. Features that do not fit — marked asymmetry, weakness out of proportion, rapid progression, autonomic or cranial involvement — suggest another diagnosis and need neurology.

Diabetes and non-diabetic hyperglycaemia; alcohol; vitamin B12 or folate deficiency; hypothyroidism; chronic kidney or liver disease; drugs and toxins; paraproteinaemia; less often vasculitis, inflammatory (CIDP) or hereditary neuropathy. Heavy alcohol use and excess weight make alcohol and diabetes the first two to test here.

HbA1c (48 mmol/mol or more is the diagnostic threshold for diabetes, WHO 2011 (international); 42–47 mmol/mol is non-diabetic hyperglycaemia, NICE PH38; management per NICE NG28 [2]); vitamin B12 and folate (NICE NG239 [1]: test when symptoms include neurological features; do not wait for anaemia); FBC and MCV; U&E and eGFR; LFTs including GGT; TFTs; ESR or CRP; serum protein electrophoresis. Neurology and nerve conduction studies if the cause is unclear, the pattern is atypical or it keeps progressing.

Rapidly ascending weakness over days, difficulty walking, breathlessness, swallowing difficulty or facial weakness suggests Guillain–Barré syndrome — same-day hospital assessment, not outpatient nerve studies. Neurological signs with B12 deficiency need prompt treatment (NICE NG239 [1]).

Ask about quantity with AUDIT (NICE CG115 [4]); low-risk guidance is no more than 14 units a week spread over 3 or more days (UK CMOs [7]). Do not advise a dependent drinker to stop suddenly — assess for dependence and plan assisted withdrawal (CG115 [4]). NICE CG100 [5]: offer prophylactic oral thiamine to harmful or dependent drinkers who are malnourished or at risk of malnutrition, have decompensated liver disease, or are in acute or planned withdrawal (dose per BNF).

Reduced sensation means injuries, burns and ulcers go unnoticed — his stubbed toe proves it. Daily foot checks, well-fitting footwear, testing bath water by hand or thermometer, and podiatry. If diabetes is confirmed, risk-stratify and refer per NICE NG19 [3].

NICE CG173 [6]: offer a choice of amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin for neuropathic pain; if the first is not effective or tolerated, offer one of the remaining three. Take care with sedating drugs and alcohol together.
DVLA [8]: he must tell the DVLA if a condition affects his ability to drive safely. If assessment confirms alcohol misuse or dependence, DVLA notification is required under the alcohol standards.

model.text: Hello Mr Oyelaran, I’m Dr Clarke. What’s brought you in today?

For the last few months my feet have felt numb and tingly, like walking on cotton wool, and it’s creeping up my legs. Now the tips of my fingers are starting too. Both sides. I stubbed my toe badly last week and barely felt it. What’s causing it, doc?
That sounds unsettling — especially not feeling that toe. I want to find out why. Can I ask some questions, go through the examination recorded in your notes, and then we’ll plan the tests together?
model.why: Acknowledges the concern and sets an agenda

model.text: Yes, go on.
Has it been slowly spreading over months, or has anything changed quickly in the last few days? Any actual weakness — tripping, dropping things, trouble with stairs?
model.why: Tempo and motor involvement — screens for Guillain–Barré and atypical features

model.text: Slowly. Months. No weakness, just the numbness.
Any trouble with breathing, swallowing or your face? Any problems with your bladder, bowels, or dizziness when you stand?
model.why: Screens bulbar, respiratory and autonomic red flags

model.text: No, none of that.

Good. Some of the common causes are to do with blood sugar, vitamins, the thyroid, and alcohol, so I ask everyone about them. Have you ever been told your sugar was high? Do you take any tablets or remedies?
Never had it checked. No tablets.
And alcohol — I’m asking because it can affect nerves, not to tell you off. What would you drink in a typical week?
model.why: Raises alcohol honestly and without judgement

model.text: (pause) More than I should, if I’m honest. Most days.

Thank you for being straight with me — that really helps. I’ll ask a few more questions about drinking in a moment, because it matters for how we cut down safely. Does anyone in your family have nerve problems like this?
model.why: Acknowledges honesty; plans AUDIT and dependence check; family history

model.text: Not that I know of.

(reviewing the recorded examination) The nurse’s foot check this morning found you couldn’t feel the fine filament at several points on both feet, and vibration was absent at both big toes — the same pattern on both sides. Your foot pulses and skin are fine. Your strength and reflexes haven’t been checked yet, so I’ll arrange that, though from what you describe your strength sounds normal. Could you hold your feet up to the camera so I can see that toe? This fits a nerve problem called a peripheral neuropathy.
model.why: Recorded foot check supports a symmetrical length-dependent sensory neuropathy; power and reflexes to be examined

model.text: So what’s causing it?
That’s the key question. Before I answer — what have you been wondering yourself? Is there anything you’re worried it might be?
model.why: Elicits ideas and concerns before explaining

model.text: I wondered if it was the drink. And I’m worried it’ll keep spreading and I’ll end up in a wheelchair.

Those are fair worries. Alcohol is one possible cause, but not the only one. High blood sugar is the commonest cause of this pattern, and low vitamin B12 or an underactive thyroid can do the same. Several of these are treatable, and treating the cause often stops it spreading. The slow, sensation-only pattern you have is the common kind, not the kind that leads quickly to weakness.
model.why: Explains the differential and addresses the wheelchair fear honestly

model.text: So what tests?

A blood test for sugar, B12 and folate, thyroid, kidneys and liver, a blood count, an inflammation marker, and a protein test that picks up a rarer cause. If the results don’t explain it, or it keeps spreading, I’ll refer you to neurology for nerve conduction tests.
model.why: Targeted investigations with a clear referral threshold

model.text: And the drinking?

Cutting down is one of the most useful things you can do for your nerves. But if you drink every day, stopping suddenly can be dangerous, so let’s go through a short questionnaire and agree a safe plan together — there’s help available if you want it. I’d also like to start a vitamin called thiamine, which nerves need.
model.why: Safe alcohol plan (AUDIT, avoid abrupt withdrawal if dependent) and thiamine

model.text: Okay. I didn’t know you could stop too fast.

Meanwhile, protect your feet. Check them every day for cuts or blisters, wear shoes that fit well, and test bath water with your hand or a thermometer, not your feet. I’ll ask a podiatrist to see you too.

If you develop weakness that spreads over days, trouble walking, breathing or swallowing, or your face goes weak, go to A&E or call 999 — that would be a different, urgent problem. Can you tell me back what we’ve agreed?
model.why: Specific Guillain–Barré safety net, then teach-back

model.text: Bloods this week. Check my feet every day. Thiamine. Cut down the drink safely — we’ll talk about it. A&E if I get weak or can’t breathe.
Exactly. Let’s book a review in two weeks for the results and the drinking plan. You did the right thing coming in.
model.why: Defined follow-up and a supportive close

model.text: Thanks, doc. That’s less scary than I thought.

social.t: People often under-report drinking when they expect judgement. A curious, non-blaming approach gets more accurate information and better engagement.
Numb feet and poor balance raise the risk of falls and injury at work and at home. Ask what his day involves once the cause is clearer.

legal.t: He must notify the DVLA if a condition affects his ability to drive safely. If alcohol misuse or dependence is confirmed, notification is required under the DVLA alcohol standards (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive).

professional.t: NICE CG115: assess dependence (AUDIT) before advising reduction; dependent drinkers need planned, assisted withdrawal rather than a sudden stop.
A cause search only works if abnormal results are acted on. Book the review before he leaves and document the neurology threshold.

community.t: Local NHS alcohol services (self-referral), Drinkline, and community podiatry for foot protection.

redFlags: Weakness spreading over days, difficulty walking — possible Guillain–Barré: same-day assessment
Breathing or swallowing difficulty, facial weakness, autonomic symptoms
Marked asymmetry, motor-predominant or rapidly progressive features — neurology
psychosocial: Alcohol intake, dependence and readiness to change
Falls and injury risk at home and work; foot care
ice: Idea: it might be the drink
Concern: it will spread and put him in a wheelchair
Expectation: a cause and a fix

playbook.diagnosis: Symmetrical, length-dependent sensory polyneuropathy (glove-and-stocking) over months, without weakness or red flags. Cause not yet known: diabetes and alcohol lead the differential, with B12/folate deficiency, hypothyroidism, renal or liver disease and paraproteinaemia to exclude.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The long nerves to your feet and hands aren’t working properly, which is why they feel numb. Something is affecting them — often blood sugar, alcohol or a vitamin — and finding which one tells us how to stop it getting worse.”

management.reflectIce: “You wondered about the drink, and you’re worried about a wheelchair. Let’s find the actual cause — several are treatable.”
management.psychosocial: Alcohol discussed without judgement; dependence assessed; safe reduction plan with support; foot safety at home.
sharedPlan: HbA1c, B12 and folate, FBC, U&E, LFT and GGT, TFT, ESR or CRP, serum protein electrophoresis
AUDIT and dependence check; thiamine; safe reduction or assisted withdrawal (NICE CG115, CG100)
Daily foot checks, footwear, water temperature, podiatry; NICE NG19 foot risk if diabetes confirmed
Neurology and nerve conduction if cause unclear, atypical or progressing
safetyNet: Spreading weakness, trouble walking, breathing or swallowing, facial weakness — A&E or 999
Results and alcohol plan review in 2 weeks

pitfalls.intro: This station is passed by a systematic hunt for the cause and failed by stopping at the label. Alcohol is the obvious lead; the examiner is watching whether you test for the others and raise it well.

items.why: The treatable causes — diabetes, B12, thyroid — are the point of the station.
items.fix: Order the targeted bloods, including HbA1c, B12/folate and protein electrophoresis.

items.fail: Blaming alcohol and testing nothing else.
items.why: Anchoring on the obvious misses diabetes, the commonest cause.
items.fix: Keep alcohol as one hypothesis and test for the others.

items.fail: Not asking about weakness, breathing or swallowing.
items.why: Guillain–Barré is rare but an emergency.
items.fix: Screen tempo and motor, bulbar and autonomic symptoms.

items.fail: Telling a daily drinker to stop at once.
items.why: Sudden withdrawal in dependence can cause seizures (NICE CG115).
items.fix: Assess dependence and plan a safe reduction or assisted withdrawal.
Explain why you ask, thank him for honesty, and offer help.

items.fail: No foot advice after he mentions an unfelt injury.
items.why: Missed ulcers and burns are the commonest harm.
items.fix: Daily checks, footwear, water temperature, podiatry.

items.why: No follow-up or referral threshold is unsafe.
items.fix: Book the review and state when you would refer to neurology.

SCA_MODELS.text: So what’s causing it?
That’s the key question. Before I answer — what have you been wondering yourself? Is there anything you’re worried it might be?
SCA_MODELS.why: Elicits ideas and concerns before explaining

SCA_MODELS.text: I wondered if it was the drink. And I’m worried it’ll keep spreading and I’ll end up in a wheelchair.

Those are fair worries. Alcohol is one possible cause, but not the only one. High blood sugar is the commonest cause of this pattern, and low vitamin B12 or an underactive thyroid can do the same. Several of these are treatable, and treating the cause often stops it spreading. The slow, sensation-only pattern you have is the common kind, not the kind that leads quickly to weakness.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains the differential and addresses the wheelchair fear honestly

SCA_MODELS.text: So what tests?

A blood test for sugar, B12 and folate, thyroid, kidneys and liver, a blood count, an inflammation marker, and a protein test that picks up a rarer cause. If the results don’t explain it, or it keeps spreading, I’ll refer you to neurology for nerve conduction tests.
SCA_MODELS.why: Targeted investigations with a clear referral threshold

SCA_MODELS.text: And the drinking?

Cutting down is one of the most useful things you can do for your nerves. But if you drink every day, stopping suddenly can be dangerous, so let’s go through a short questionnaire and agree a safe plan together — there’s help available if you want it. I’d also like to start a vitamin called thiamine, which nerves need.
SCA_MODELS.why: Safe alcohol plan (AUDIT, avoid abrupt withdrawal if dependent) and thiamine

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. I didn’t know you could stop too fast.

Meanwhile, protect your feet. Check them every day for cuts or blisters, wear shoes that fit well, and test bath water with your hand or a thermometer, not your feet. I’ll ask a podiatrist to see you too.

If you develop weakness that spreads over days, trouble walking, breathing or swallowing, or your face goes weak, go to A&E or call 999 — that would be a different, urgent problem. Can you tell me back what we’ve agreed?
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific Guillain–Barré safety net, then teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: Bloods this week. Check my feet every day. Thiamine. Cut down the drink safely — we’ll talk about it. A&E if I get weak or can’t breathe.
Exactly. Let’s book a review in two weeks for the results and the drinking plan. You did the right thing coming in.
SCA_MODELS.why: Defined follow-up and a supportive close

SCA_MODELS.text: Thanks, doc. That’s less scary than I thought.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE NG239 (vitamin B12 deficiency in over 16s, 2024) · [2] NICE NG28 (type 2 diabetes in adults, updated) · [3] NICE NG19 (diabetic foot problems, 2015, updated) · [4] NICE CG115 (alcohol-use disorders: diagnosis, assessment and management of harmful drinking and alcohol dependence, 2011) · [5] NICE CG100 (alcohol-use disorders: physical complications, 2010, updated) · [6] NICE CG173 (neuropathic pain in adults: pharmacological management in non-specialist settings, 2013, updated 2020) · [7] UK Chief Medical Officers’ low-risk drinking guidelines (2016) · [8] DVLA Assessing fitness to drive: a guide for medical professionals (current edition)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Symmetrical numbness and tingling that starts in the feet, climbs the legs and then reaches the fingertips is a length-dependent sensory polyneuropathy — the glove-and-stocking pattern. The label is the easy part. The station is about finding the cause (diabetes, alcohol, B12 or folate deficiency, thyroid, kidney or liver disease, drugs, paraprotein), screening for the rare emergency (Guillain–Barré), protecting his numb feet, and talking about alcohol without judgement.

points.t: Distal, symmetrical, feet before hands, slowly progressive over months, sensory more than motor: a length-dependent polyneuropathy. Features that do not fit — marked asymmetry, weakness out of proportion, rapid progression, autonomic or cranial involvement — suggest another diagnosis and need neurology.

Diabetes and non-diabetic hyperglycaemia; alcohol; vitamin B12 or folate deficiency; hypothyroidism; chronic kidney or liver disease; drugs and toxins; paraproteinaemia; less often vasculitis, inflammatory (CIDP) or hereditary neuropathy. Heavy alcohol use and excess weight make alcohol and diabetes the first two to test here.

HbA1c (48 mmol/mol or more is the diagnostic threshold for diabetes, WHO 2011 (international); 42–47 mmol/mol is non-diabetic hyperglycaemia, NICE PH38; management per NICE NG28 [2]); vitamin B12 and folate (NICE NG239 [1]: test when symptoms include neurological features; do not wait for anaemia); FBC and MCV; U&E and eGFR; LFTs including GGT; TFTs; ESR or CRP; serum protein electrophoresis. Neurology and nerve conduction studies if the cause is unclear, the pattern is atypical or it keeps progressing.

Rapidly ascending weakness over days, difficulty walking, breathlessness, swallowing difficulty or facial weakness suggests Guillain–Barré syndrome — same-day hospital assessment, not outpatient nerve studies. Neurological signs with B12 deficiency need prompt treatment (NICE NG239 [1]).

Ask about quantity with AUDIT (NICE CG115 [4]); low-risk guidance is no more than 14 units a week spread over 3 or more days (UK CMOs [7]). Do not advise a dependent drinker to stop suddenly — assess for dependence and plan assisted withdrawal (CG115 [4]). NICE CG100 [5]: offer prophylactic oral thiamine to harmful or dependent drinkers who are malnourished or at risk of malnutrition, have decompensated liver disease, or are in acute or planned withdrawal (dose per BNF).

Reduced sensation means injuries, burns and ulcers go unnoticed — his stubbed toe proves it. Daily foot checks, well-fitting footwear, testing bath water by hand or thermometer, and podiatry. If diabetes is confirmed, risk-stratify and refer per NICE NG19 [3].

NICE CG173 [6]: offer a choice of amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin for neuropathic pain; if the first is not effective or tolerated, offer one of the remaining three. Take care with sedating drugs and alcohol together.
DVLA [8]: he must tell the DVLA if a condition affects his ability to drive safely. If assessment confirms alcohol misuse or dependence, DVLA notification is required under the alcohol standards.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let him describe the pattern and the stubbed toe in his own words.
Explored alcohol (non-judgemental, with AUDIT planned), weight, medication and family history.
Picked up ‘barely felt it’ as a foot-safety cue and ‘what’s causing it’ as his main agenda.
Idea: maybe the drink. Concern: spreading to a wheelchair. Expectation: a cause and a fix.
Sensation (touch, pinprick, vibration, proprioception), reflexes, power, gait and Romberg, feet; targeted bloods.
Length-dependent sensory polyneuropathy; tested against mononeuropathy, radiculopathy, central causes and Guillain–Barré.
Asked about tempo, weakness, bulbar, respiratory and autonomic symptoms; knew GBS needs same-day assessment.
Symmetrical glove-and-stocking sensory neuropathy; cause to be found — diabetes and alcohol lead.
HbA1c, B12/folate, FBC, U&E, LFT/GGT, TFT, ESR/CRP, protein electrophoresis; thiamine; neurology if unclear or progressing.
Addressed alcohol safely (dependence check, no abrupt stop if dependent) and weight; foot care and podiatry.
999/A&E for spreading weakness, breathing or swallowing problems; review in 2 weeks; teach-back.

social.t: People often under-report drinking when they expect judgement. A curious, non-blaming approach gets more accurate information and better engagement.
Numb feet and poor balance raise the risk of falls and injury at work and at home. Ask what his day involves once the cause is clearer.

legal.t: He must notify the DVLA if a condition affects his ability to drive safely. If alcohol misuse or dependence is confirmed, notification is required under the DVLA alcohol standards (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive).

professional.t: NICE CG115: assess dependence (AUDIT) before advising reduction; dependent drinkers need planned, assisted withdrawal rather than a sudden stop.
A cause search only works if abnormal results are acted on. Book the review before he leaves and document the neurology threshold.

community.t: Local NHS alcohol services (self-referral), Drinkline, and community podiatry for foot protection.

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Symmetrical, length-dependent sensory polyneuropathy (glove-and-stocking) over months, without weakness or red flags. Cause not yet known: diabetes and alcohol lead the differential, with B12/folate deficiency, hypothyroidism, renal or liver disease and paraproteinaemia to exclude.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The long nerves to your feet and hands aren’t working properly, which is why they feel numb. Something is affecting them — often blood sugar, alcohol or a vitamin — and finding which one tells us how to stop it getting worse.”

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is passed by a systematic hunt for the cause and failed by stopping at the label. Alcohol is the obvious lead; the examiner is watching whether you test for the others and raise it well.

items.why: The treatable causes — diabetes, B12, thyroid — are the point of the station.
items.fix: Order the targeted bloods, including HbA1c, B12/folate and protein electrophoresis.

items.fail: Blaming alcohol and testing nothing else.
items.why: Anchoring on the obvious misses diabetes, the commonest cause.
items.fix: Keep alcohol as one hypothesis and test for the others.

items.fail: Not asking about weakness, breathing or swallowing.
items.why: Guillain–Barré is rare but an emergency.
items.fix: Screen tempo and motor, bulbar and autonomic symptoms.

items.fail: Telling a daily drinker to stop at once.
items.why: Sudden withdrawal in dependence can cause seizures (NICE CG115).
items.fix: Assess dependence and plan a safe reduction or assisted withdrawal.
Explain why you ask, thank him for honesty, and offer help.

items.fail: No foot advice after he mentions an unfelt injury.
items.why: Missed ulcers and burns are the commonest harm.
items.fix: Daily checks, footwear, water temperature, podiatry.

items.why: No follow-up or referral threshold is unsafe.
items.fix: Book the review and state when you would refer to neurology.
